To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the development of hepatic encepahalopathy (HE), due to galactosaemia‐induced acute hepatic failure in rabbits, was associated with an increase in the density of receptors for inhibitory neurotransmitters and a decrease in the receptor density for excitatory neurotransmitters.
the density of GABA receptors increases, and the densities of glutamate, aspartate, and kainic receptors decrease in HE.
the number of neurotransmitter receptors in the brain changes in a predictable way in a rabbit model of hepatic coma.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the pathophysiological basis of hepatic encepahalopathy, a syndrome which occurs in many types of acute liver failure.
the pathophysiology of hepatic encepahalopathy, a common complication of acute and chronic liver disease, and the mechanisms of its treatment.
the study of the pathogenesis of hepatic encephaopathy, a neuropsychiatric complication of liver failure.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the changes observed in the status of neurotransmitter receptors in the brain of rabbits in HE are consistent with a pathophysiology that could mediate the neural inhibition of the syndrome.
HE may be associated in part with a decreased sensitivity to excitotoxins, and in part with an enhanced sensitivity to glycine.

the brain in HE is in a state of hyperexcitability, which may be due to a decreased sensitivity to the excitatory neurotransmitters, glutamate and aspartate, and an increased sensitivity to the inhibitory neurotransmitters, glycine and GABA.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the changes in the status of neurotransmitter receptors observed in the present study may be important in the development of HE.
in HE, the inhibitory neurotransmitters are over‐expressed and the excitatory neurotransmitters are under‐expressed.
in HE the inhibitory neurotransmitters are over‐active and the excitatory neurotransmitters are under‐active.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the brain is not a static structure, but rather a dynamic one that is continuously changing and adapting to its environment.
